# Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration

https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10408-8

Received: 30 June 2025

Accepted: 12 March 2026

Published online: 22 April 2026

Check for updates

Kaixuan Li $^{1,2,8}$ , Jianfeng Chen $^{2,8}$ , Huizeng Li $^{1✉}$ , An Li $^{1}$ , Xiaoyu Hou $^{1,3}$ , Sujuan Ma $^{1}$ , Maoxiong Zhao $^{4}$ , Shengnan Chen $^{1}$ , Quan Liu $^{1,3}$ , Dongyu Yang $^{1,3}$ , Rujun Li $^{1}$ , Xiao Deng $^{1}$ , Renxuan Yuan $^{1,3}$ , Luanluan Xue $^{1}$ , Wanling Liu $^{1,3}$ , Ming Yang $^{1}$ , Zhimei Jia $^{1}$ , Mingzhu Li $^{3,5}$ , Joel K. W. Yang $^{6}$ , Cheng-Wei Qiu $^{2,7✉}$ & Yanlin Song $^{1,3✉}$

Biological systems achieve multifunctionality through the synergy of nanoscale building blocks and microscale morphological hierarchies, a multiscale structure that would be advantageous to implement in metamaterials $^{1-5}$ . However, most artificial optical systems can only be fabricated on a single scale, facing the challenges of limited scalability, inadequate tunability and monotonous functionality $^{6-8}$ . Here we present a printable meta-assembly strategy that enables the fabrication of multiscale hierarchical optical architectures through continuous roll-to-roll (R2R) manufacturing. The meta-assembly comprises low-cost polystyrene (PS) nanoparticles periodically embedded in a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix, forming a nanolattice-based microconcave optical interface that enables precise integration of guided-wave and reflected-wave dispersion and interference $^{9-12}$ . By optical coupling, distinct synergetic colouration is explored and experimentally realized with high designability and tunability. Overcoming scalability constraints, metre-scale meta-assembly prints with single-pixel customization can be rapidly fabricated from the nanoscale building blocks, spanning seven orders of magnitude in length. The vibrant prints exhibit controlled colour separation and integration performances, along with environmental stability, showing potential for eco-friendly colouration, intelligent displays and information security. This work provides a versatile methodology for biologically inspired metamaterial construction by means of multiscale photonics research.

Colour, the most intuitive visual signature of the world, underpins fundamental interactions in biology $^{13,14}$ , technology $^{15,16}$ and culture $^{17,18}$ . Its origins lie in the light–matter interactions across multilength scales, which can be broadly categorized into chemical pigmentation colour (molecular absorption) and structural colour (optical interference/diffraction by microscale/nanoscale architectures) $^{2}$ . Although chemical dyes have dominated applications for millennia, the limitations of toxic chemical pollution $^{19-22}$ and colour fading $^{23,24}$ still persist as pressing challenges. Thus, structural colour, as an eco-friendly colouration alternative, has emerged as a focal point in cutting-edge science and transformative technology, showcasing substantial potential to address both environmental and functional imperatives $^{25-29}$ .

Nature stands as the quintessential architect of structural colouration, demonstrating elegant optical systems through hierarchical coupling of multiscale microstructures/nanostructures $^{2,5,30}$ and endowing organisms with resplendent chromatic displays and diverse crucial ecological functions $^{31-34}$ . Typical examples are Morpho butterflies $^{35}$ and Saharan ants $^{36}$ , which have evolved sophisticated hierarchical architectures that can synergize several optical effects (interference, scattering and so on) for brilliant colouration, alongside excellent heterosexual attraction and survival capabilities. Despite decades of inspiration from the biological blueprints, translating these into artificial realizations remains highly challenging $^{37,38}$ , mainly because of the lack of validated multiscale optical models with scalable fabrication capability. Present artificial colouration systems struggle to predict multiscale synergetic interactions or unify disparate chromogenic mechanisms $^{38-40}$ , thus failing to guide the rational design of hierarchical colouration structures. Meanwhile, nanofabrication strategies for hierarchical architectures (for example, two-photon lithography) face critical trade-offs among cost, efficiency and scalability $^{37,41-44}$ . Consequently, a unified multiscale optical platform with versatile fabrication is highly desirable.

In this work, we present a printable meta-assembly strategy that enables the scalable fabrication of multiscale hierarchical optical architectures with distinct synergetic colouration performance. The meta-assembly model is designed with a microscale hemispherical

configuration composed of hexagonal close-packed nanoparticles, forming a nanolattice-based microconcave interface. The nanolattice first defines a wavelength-selective photonic bandgap (PBG) $^{9}$ and the curved interface with refractive index contrast subsequently endows the meta-assembly with light localization capability by means of total internal reflections (TIRs) $^{10}$ (Supplementary Figs. 1–3; see Supplementary Discussions for details). Through the ordered nano-arrangement on the curved interface, the meta-assembly achieves efficient multiscale optical interplay, enabling substantial field enhancement and dispersion in a single unit (Supplementary Fig. 4). Then, to prepare the meta-assembly in batch, we develop a combined methodology called roll-to-roll additive nanoprinting (R2R-ANP) and a tailored manufacturing set-up, achieving the scalable and customized meta-assembly printing (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1).

Figure 1a demonstrates the key R2R-ANP steps, including on-demand inkjet printing, blade coating and embedded transfer. First, digital images are designed into printing patterns, of which the spatial arrangement, size and density can be set as required with single-pixel resolution (Supplementary Fig. 5). Then, using inkjet printing, the PS nanoparticle ink is precisely deposited on a hydrophobic and low-adhesion substrate to construct domed colloidal photonic crystals (DCPCs). The PS nanoparticles are selected as the building blocks owing to the matched refractive index, scalable synthesis capability and excellent stability that are essential for scalable R2R-ANP (Supplementary Figs. 6 and 7). After the ink dries, PS nanoparticles (for example, 216 nm in diameter) will self-assemble into the DCPC structures with green structural colour. Subsequently, a layer of liquid PDMS is blade-coated on the DCPCs and cured by thermal polymerization. Here the DCPCs are stably embedded in the PDMS matrix and interconnected using cross-linked networks. Finally, on peeling and rolling the PDMS off the substrate, the interface profiles transform from domed to concave, thereby triggering the meta-assembly formation and size-dependent rim-centre co-colouration. Consequently, the initially green prints exhibit rich colouration (Fig. 1a, bottom and Supplementary Fig. 8).

Spanning from nanoscale building blocks to microscale meta-assemblies, mesoscale arrays, and macroscale prints, the R2R-ANP approach bridges seven orders of magnitude in length, achieving the large-scale manufacturing of multiscale optical architectures (Fig. 1b). Figure 1c shows the multiscale optical effects in the meta-assembly model. At the nanoscale, the periodic arrangement of PS nanoparticles ( $n_{\text{PS}} = 1.59$ ) within the PDMS matrix ( $n_{\text{PDMS}} = 1.41$ ) generates the PBG effect, inducing the wavelength-selective reflection and central colouration. Meanwhile, the concave optical interface confines the incident light to propagate along the curved trajectories, guiding multibounce interference and colouration at the rim region. Thus, the electric fields are spatially resolved and enhanced, manifesting distinct wavelength-dependent localization (Fig. 1d). Furthermore, owing to phase retardation by TIR $^{45}$ , the capability of polarization conversion is introduced into the meta-assembly system (Supplementary Fig. 9), yielding annular imaging under crossed polarizers. Notably, in contrast to photonic-crystal microspheres (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Figs. 10 and 11) and homogeneous polymer hemispheres (Supplementary Fig. 12), the meta-assembly exclusively exhibits a unique multiscale optical effect that is absent in these control samples. Moreover, this optical performance demonstrates versatile tunability (Fig. 1f), with the TIR-based reflection shifting as the meta-assembly size increases.

## Principles for scalable R2R-ANP

As is well known, scalable fabrication imposes stringent demands on the throughput, yield and uniformity of the entire manufacturing process, with the following key issues being critical for scalable R2R-ANP (Fig. 2a). First and foremost, continuous inkjet printing is essential. Although inkjet printing provides on-demand patterning capabilities, it imposes stringent requirements on ink properties (for example, viscosities, surface tensions, boiling points) $^{46}$ . To mitigate unstable jetting and nozzle clogging problems, we optimize the formamide-based colloidal ink (Supplementary Fig. 13), achieving stable, high-speed and high-resolution printing (Supplementary Figs. 14–16). Next, to freely construct the DCPC structure, ink droplets are designed to deposit on the hydrophobic and low-adhesion substrates (Fig. 2a, (1)), characterized by a large receding contact angle ( $\theta_{Rec} \approx 90^{\circ}$ ). On such substrates, the ink droplets can continuously shrink at a constant $\theta_{Rec}$ , driving nanoparticles to self-assemble into DCPC structures, which are readily tuned by controlling nanoparticle concentration and printed ink-drop layers (Extended Data Fig. 2). Meanwhile, the optimal $\theta_{Rec}$ window for high-performance meta-assembly ranges from $80^{\circ}$ to $110^{\circ}$ , within which the meta-assemblies show pronounced rim enhancement (Fig. 2b). Furthermore, to expedite solvent evaporation, the substrate temperature is maintained at $50^{\circ}C$ throughout the processing. By using these optimized parameters, tens of millions of DCPCs with high resolution (403,225 dots per square inch) and exceptional uniformity are successfully fabricated (Supplementary Fig. 17), establishing a solid foundation for high-performance meta-assemblies.

The following critical step involves the construction of stable microconcave optical interfaces. For pure nanoparticle assemblies, they exhibit inherent fragility owing to weak inter-particle interactions. Thus, we design the composite optical interfaces by introducing PDMS matrix. Experimentally, the PDMS prepolymer is directly coated onto the DCPC surface. Thanks to its low surface energy, the prepolymer can freely diffuse into the voids between the nanoparticles and encapsulate the DCPCs while fully preserving the ordered nano-arrangements and domed morphology (Fig. 2a, (2)). On prepolymer curing, the nanoparticles can be stably fixed by cross-linked networks, forming an integral composite that is embedded in the PDMS matrix (Fig. 2a, (3)). Thus, with the PDMS film peeled from the substrate and flipped, the meta-assemblies with robust optical interfaces directly form (Fig. 2a, (4)). Using this embedded transfer, all fabricated DCPCs can be converted into meta-assemblies with a $100\%$ yield, regardless of their number, size and distribution (Fig. 2c). Furthermore, the as-prepared meta-assemblies feature excellent size and colour uniformity (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 18), demonstrating great large-area potential. Experimentally, we fabricate a metre-scale film containing more than 40 million meta-assemblies, with the total number of nanoparticles exceeding $7 \times 10^{13}$ , which effectively validates the scalability of our strategy (Fig. 2e). Furthermore, apart from circular meta-assemblies, diverse topological meta-assemblies can be readily fabricated by integrating R2R-ANP with heterogeneous wettability design (Supplementary Fig. 19 and Extended Data Fig. 3), greatly enriching the geometric diversity.

## Optical synergies in meta-assembly systems

To exactly reveal the synergetic optical effects, a numerical analysis is performed on the basis of the built meta-assembly model. Given the mismatch between hexagonal lattice and curved hemisphere, we have first smoothed the interface perturbations, using an ordered nanolattice interface on the premise of computational accuracy. Unlike the predictable optical effects of single-scale structures, the meta-assembly enables non-trivial modulation of electromagnetic field distribution and light propagation. As illustrated in Fig. 3a–f, wavelength-dependent field enhancement and mode competition occur at the interface, owing to the interplay between different-scaled optical effects. Briefly, when the incident wavelength ( $\lambda_{in}$ ) falls outside the PBG range ( $\lambda_{PBG}$ ), field enhancement is only observed in the interface region by means of TIR confinement (Fig. 3a,c). By contrast, when $\lambda_{in}$ falls within the $\lambda_{PBG}$ range, the field of the central region is enhanced (Fig. 3b). Owing to the coexistence and interplay of multiscale optical effects, the meta-assembly system exhibits distinctive dispersion characteristics. As illustrated in the near-field to far-field dispersion profile (Fig. 3i,j), the central colouration is essentially invariant owing to strong wavelength selectivity and minimal angular dispersion, whereas the rim region exhibits a pronounced angular-dependent colour variation. Rim dispersion originates from the pronounced optical path difference during TIR-confined propagation when light impinges on the rim regions, thereby inducing the mutual interference of electromagnetic waves. Because short wavelengths first meet the interference condition, their intensities are preferentially enhanced (for example, blue and purple). As the optical path difference increases, the interference of long wavelengths is enhanced, with yellow, orange and similar hues gradually emerging. Notably, owing to the filtering effect by PBGs, the corresponding intensity is largely suppressed. In the near field, this wavelength dependence is indistinguishable. As the wave propagates into the far-field region, the interfacial confinement gradually attenuates, whereas the spatial phase coherence of the scattered light is markedly enhanced. Consequently, the optical field distribution becomes stably established, with the specific wavelength components exhibiting a more uniform propagation direction. Correspondingly, the meta-assembly shows a constant PBG-dominated reflection in the central region and intense wavelength-dependent scattering near the interface, causing the spatially varied colour distribution. To illustrate this colour variation, we have compiled all reflected spectra and projected them onto a single plane using spectrum-to-colour conversion (Fig. 3k,l).

## Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly

Notably, the pronounced multiscale optical interplay within the meta-assembly system offers a facile approach to tailoring its structural colouration. Accordingly, we collect the spectral data at specific spatial regions of the meta-assembly and convert the spectra into intuitive chromatic colours, first illustrating the distinct colour synergy from parts to the whole. Subsequently, the colour tunability corresponding to structural changes is systematically demonstrated. As shown in Fig. 4a, reducing the meta-assembly diameter ( $D_{m}$ ) from $80 \times D_{n}$ to $40 \times D_{n}$ (in which $D_{n}$ is the photonic lattice constant, 220 nm) triggers a distinct rim colour transition from orange to blue owing to the changed TIR paths, whereas the central colour remains green. Accordingly, the overall colour shifts slightly from yellowish green to cyan. Conversely, increasing $D_{n}$ from 220 nm to 240 nm ( $D_{m} = 40 \times D_{n}$ ) triggers a prominent redshift in the central colour and a slight modulation on the rim colour owing to the changed photonic lattice. At this time, the overall colour is vividly shifted from cyan–green to pink. Such multiscale colour modulation can be further validated in the meta-assemblies with different multiscale structural parameters (Fig. 4b). Moreover, to fully illustrate the quantitative correspondence between colour and multiscale structures, we construct the centre, rim and overall colouration libraries with varied $D_{m}$ and $D_{n}$ (Fig. 4c) and experimentally map the meta-assemblies from the microscale (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 4) and macroscale (Supplementary Fig. 21), directly illustrating the structure–colour correlation. As shown, the centre colour exhibits a clear linear dependence on $D_{n}$ , with a distinct redshift observed as the $D_{n}$ increases. Furthermore, the rim colour gradually shifts from short-wavelength hues (for example, blue and purple) to long-wavelength hues (for example, orange and red) as the $D_{m}$ increases. Because the colour variations at the rim and centre both contribute to the overall colouration, the meta-assembly naturally features the multiscale tunability, thus enabling broadband and refined colour modulation.

Besides tailoring structural parameters, the meta-assembly-based macroscopic colouration also exhibits printing-enabled tunability (Fig. 4e–h and Extended Data Fig. 5). First, the reflection intensity is facile to adjust with the regulation of meta-assembly density (Supplementary Fig. 22). Second, meta-assemblies with different $D_{n}$ and $D_{m}$ can be integrated and printed to achieve the predefined macroscopic colour mixing. As shown in Fig. 4e–g, through multinozzle inkjet printing of different nanoparticle inks, the meta-assemblies with characteristic red, green and blue central colours are patterned in an orderly manner, yielding the macroscopic white colouration. Furthermore, through designed layer-by-layer processing, the meta-assemblies with different sizes can be readily integrated using a single nanoparticle ink, enabling the facile fabrication of colourful panel and print (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Overall, the combined structural and printing tunability endows the meta-assembly system with full-scale colour designability, thus showcasing substantial potential for custom-tailored structural-colour applications.

chunks.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
chunks.text:
## Macroscopic synergetic colouration

Not only in individual meta-assemblies, the synergetic colouration can also be readily scaled up to the macroscale by controlling the illumination conditions. As illustrated in Fig. 5a,b, with an oblique light incidence into the meta-assembly, the PBG-dominated Bragg reflection and TIR-dominated retroreflection will be spatially separated, thereby inducing the colour separation at the macroscale. This illumination-controlled reflection and retroreflection afford the macroscopic meta-assembly colouration with enhanced tunability, for which the colour output can be precisely modulated by tailoring the Bragg angle ( $\theta$ , reflection mode) and the light-viewing distance (D, retroreflection mode). Notably, when the single oblique incident beam is switched to dual-beam cooperative illumination, the reflection and retroreflection can be effectively integrated to achieve the mode combination and colour mixing. As shown in Fig. 5c, the reflective green and retroreflective blue are uniformly mixed, inducing the cyan generation. Using different-sized meta-assemblies, a rich palette of mixed structural colours is achieved (Supplementary Fig. 23). Especially, when the print composed of patterned meta-assemblies is applied, it can yield a more intriguing synergetic colouration (Fig. 5d). The print is specifically designed with dual-sized meta-assemblies (13 and 30 $\mu$ m in diameter) that are composed of the 216-nm-diameter nanoparticles. In reflection mode, the print only exhibits an overall uniform green image. By contrast, the retroreflection mode yields a colourful appearance arising from the TIR-based size-dependent colouration. Finally, under dual-beam cooperative illumination, the reflection and retroreflection are simultaneously excited and superimposed, inducing gradational chromatic colours and a soft visual appearance.

The unique synergetic colouration endows the meta-assemblies with substantial potential in security identification. To further validate its real-world applicability, we systematically characterize the stability of meta-assemblies against light irradiation, thermal stress, solvent exposure, washing and mechanical deformation. Benefiting from the robust bonding between nanoparticles and the PDMS matrix, the meta-assemblies exhibit remarkable overall environmental and mechanical stabilities (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 24). Notably, the meta-assembly prints can be conformally attached to various substrates, including paper, microchips and curved glass surfaces, which are highly advantageous for the reliable and durable security functionality (Supplementary Fig. 25).

chunks.heading: Conclusions
chunks.text:
## Conclusions

In summary, we have presented a unified metamaterial platform featuring scalable fabrication capability and multiscale structural designability, enabling the customized and low-cost manufacturing of hierarchical optical architectures. The developed meta-assembly model endows the common polymer building blocks with multiscale optical activity, achieving effective optical coupling and synergetic colouration within a single unit. Its facile configuration, coupled with a tailored R2R-ANP protocol, yields the continuous R2R production of macroscopic meta-assembly prints with single-pixel resolution, thus offering a feasible route for the lab-to-fab translation of optical metamaterials. Moreover, the meta-assembly prints enable a more straightforward realization of synergistic optical performance while featuring excellent stability, thus offering substantial application potential for practical colouration scenarios ranging from information security to intelligent displays. Collectively, this printable meta-assembly strategy resolves the trade-off between optical functionality and engineering performance, providing key insights for multiscale photonics research. Furthermore, integrating intrinsic material properties into the meta-assembly model holds great promise for unlocking more intriguing functionalities.

## Materials

Styrene (99.0%), acrylic acid (98.0%), methyl methacrylate (99.9%), sodium dodecyl benzene sulfonate (95.0%), ammonium bicarbonate (99.0%), ammonium peroxodisulfate (APS, 99.0%), caustic soda (NaOH, 96.0%), acetic acid (98.0%) and hexadecane (98.0%) were purchased from J&K Scientific. Double-throw silicon wafers were purchased from Tianjin Institute of Semiconductor Technology. 1H,1H,2H, 2H-perfluorodecyltrimethoxysilane (97.0%), triethoxy-n-octylsilane (97.0%), n-decyltrichlorosilane (97.0%) and (3-glycidoxypropyl)trimethoxysilane (97.0%) were purchased from TCI. Acetone (99.0%), ethanol (99.0%) and ethylene glycol (99.0%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. PDMS (SYLGARD 184) and nigrosine powder was from Sigma-Aldrich.

chunks.heading: Preparing monodispersed core-shell PS nanoparticles
chunks.text:
## Preparing monodispersed core-shell PS nanoparticles

PS nanospheres with core–shell structure were synthesized by the one-step emulsion polymerization method. Briefly, styrene (38.0 g), acrylic acid (2.0 g) and methyl methacrylate (2.0 g) were dispersed in 160 ml of water. 0–0.011 mmol emulsifier sodium dodecyl benzene sulfonate (lower than the critical micelle concentration) and 12.50 mmol of buffer agent of ammonium bicarbonate was dissolved previously. The reaction mixture was kept at 70 °C for 0.5 h. Aqueous solution of APS as the initiator was added separately three times (24 ml, 8 ml, 8 ml of 4.25 mmol) and stirring was maintained at 80 °C for 1.5 h. Then the temperature was increased to 80 °C before the second addition of APS and was reacted for another 2 h. Finally, the polymerization reaction was carried out at 80 °C for 2 h with continuous stirring for the third addition of APS solution. The resulting particles were centrifuged (taking the supernatant, 8,000 rpm, 20 min) several times to wash away the excess polymer.

Formulating stabilized and dispersed colloidal nanoparticle ink

The colloidal particle supernatant was first concentrated by high-speed centrifugation (12,000 rpm, 20 min) and then dispersed in the solvent of formamide by ultrasonication (40 Hz, 30 min). The mass concentrations of the colloidal nanoparticles, ranging from 0.5 to 40 wt%, were adjusted by controlling the added solvent mass. The nanoparticle ink exhibits suitable printing parameters (such as viscosity: 3.84 mPa s, surface tension: 57.31 mN m $^{-1}$ , boiling point: 210 °C).

chunks.heading: Fabricating hydrophobic and low-adhesion substrates
chunks.text:
## Fabricating hydrophobic and low-adhesion substrates

The substrates with smooth surface were sequentially sonicated in methanol, acetone and deionized water for 15 min and then blow-dried with nitrogen. To increase the surface energy, the substrates were treated with air plasma (DT02S, OPS Plasma Technology Co., Ltd.) at 200 W for 200 s. Then the superhydrophilic substrates were surface-modified with different molecules, such as the 1H,1H,2H, 2H-perfluorodecyltrimethoxysilane, (3-glycidoxypropyl)trimethoxysilane and triethoxy-n-octylsilane by chemical vapour deposition at 80 °C for 3 h. Finally, the modified hydrophobic substrates were immersed in ethanol for 2 h, blow-dried with nitrogen to remove the physically deposited molecules and stored in Petri dishes.

chunks.heading: Fabricating heterogeneous wettability substrates
chunks.text:
## Fabricating heterogeneous wettability substrates

The preparation process of heterogeneous wettability consists of the following steps. First, photolithography is used to prepare the patterned substrates, with the photoresist pattern serving as hydrophilic pins. The substrate is then subjected to an overall hydrophilic treatment, so that the surface of the unpatterned region is grafted with hydrophilic groups. Finally, using the strategy of gas-phase grafting of hydrophobic molecules, the hydrophilic regions can be converted into the hydrophobic regions that are combined with the hydrophilic pins into heterogeneous wettability.

chunks.heading: Fabricating black background
chunks.text:
## Fabricating black background

The black background was prepared by doping commercial PDMS with the black dye nigrosine. First, the PDMS prepolymer and curing agent were mixed thoroughly and homogenously dispersed at a mass ratio of 10:1. Then nigrosine powder (Sigma-Aldrich) was added as the black dye at a mass fraction of 2 wt% relative to the PDMS prepolymer. Finally, the well-dispersed mixture was cast onto the back surface of the printed film and cured at 80 °C for 2 h, yielding a smooth, flat and uniform black PDMS background.

chunks.heading: Printing DCPCs
chunks.text:
## Printing DCPCs

The designed pattern was based on the binary bitmap. Controlled by the digital designed pattern, the colloidal ink was printed on the hydrophobic and low-adhesion substrate with the inkjet printing technology (independent R&D and customization) to form the domed microdroplets. After printing, the substrate was placed in situ and dried at room temperature (25 °C) to ensure the free movement of three-phase contact line and ordered self-assembly of the colloidal nanoparticles.

chunks.heading: Coating PDMS polymer matrix
chunks.text:
## Coating PDMS polymer matrix

Prepolymer of PDMS (SYLGARD 184 silicone elastomer kit, Dow) was prepared by mixing the monomers with the curing agent (with a mass ratio of 10:1) and stirred by a mechanical stirrer for 10 min. To remove the air bubbles, the prepolymer was centrifuged (3,000 rpm, 5 min). Then the prepolymer was printed on the surface of the nano-assemblies by blade and left for 5 min, allowing the prepolymer to spread and fully penetrate the voids between the nanoparticles. The thickness of the PDMS was controlled by adjusting the volume of the prepolymer.

chunks.heading: Curing the PDMS prepolymer
chunks.text:
## Curing the PDMS prepolymer

The PDMS prepolymer was continuously irradiated for 10 min by the lamps (Philips, 250 W). With the polymerization of PDMS, the nano-assemblies would automatically form a robust composite unit with the polymer network.

chunks.heading: Peeling off the cured PDMS
chunks.text:
## Peeling off the cured PDMS

The cured PDMS was directly peeled off from the substrate. As the PDMS was peeled and flipped, the meta-assemblies would be immediately formed. In the R2R-ANP process, large-scale meta-assembly patterns were rolled up by wheel curling.

chunks.heading: Experimental details during R2R processing
chunks.text:
## Experimental details during R2R processing

Inkjet printing: nozzle diameter (25 $\mu$ m), inter-nozzle spacing (100 $\mu$ m), droplet volume (10 pl), printing speed (2 mm s $^{-1}$ ), jetting frequency (0.5–20.0 Hz), droplet drying temperature (70 °C); PDMS blading: blade gap (0.5 mm), blade height (1.5 mm), blading speed (2 mm s $^{-1}$ ); thermal curing: curing temperature (180 °C), curing time per unit length (5 s cm $^{-1}$ ); peeling: peeling angle (45°), peeling speed (2 mm s $^{-1}$ ), applied pressure (0.1 MPa); rolling: winding tension (5 N), winding speed (synchronized with the printing speed, 3 mm s $^{-1}$ ). To enable high-efficiency R2R printing, the following details should be noted, including: preheating of the set-up to ensure rapid solvent evaporation and PDMS curing; presetting the module speeds to ensure coordination among various processing sections; overall cleanliness of the set-up to prevent optical defects.

chunks.heading: Microscopic optical intensity test and normalization
chunks.raw_heading: Microscopic optical intensity test and normalization
chunks.semantic_heading: Microscopic optical intensity test and normalization
chunks.text:
## Microscopic optical intensity test and normalization

Microscale optical intensity measurements were performed using standard bright-field microscopy photography (Nikon ECLIPSE Ti) and image processing. First, the reflection meta-assembly images were captured under identical illumination conditions and exposure time. Then the intensity values were quantitatively extracted through image processing and normalized against the maximum and minimum values among the images. The maximum reflectance intensity of the tested samples was scaled to 1 as the upper reference and the minimum reflectance intensity was defined as 0 as the lower reference.

chunks.heading: Macroscopic optical performance test
chunks.text:
## Macroscopic optical performance test

Macroscopic images were taken by placing the sample on a black background. Furthermore, the protective layer, such as PDMS, was coated onto the surface of the sample to prevent contaminations. For uniform colouration, the following viewing conditions are recommended: (1) ensure collimated incident light; (2) maintain a sufficiently small distance between the observation point and the light source (typically <2 cm); (3) ensure that the observer maintains a proper distance from the sample; (4) mount the sample on a black substrate to eliminate background reflection, absorb scattered light and enhance colour contrast.

chunks.heading: Mechanical performance test
chunks.text:
## Mechanical performance test

Stretching measurements were conducted by stretching the microscopic meta-assembly pattern using a Stepper Motor Controller (Beijing J&M Technologies Co., Ltd.). The test was conducted under displacement control at a constant rate of $5 \, mm s^{-1}$ with the equivalent path length of 10 mm. Digital cameras were used to record the stretching process. Similarly, the cycles-to-failure behaviours of the meta-assembly were tested at a constant rate of $30 \, mm s^{-1}$ with cycle number of 10,000. During the test, the optical microscopy images were recorded and analysed at the initial, intermediate and final of the cycle test. Other mechanical properties, such as bending and twisting, are verified directly by manual operations and recorded in real time by the digital camera.

chunks.heading: Stability tests
chunks.text:
## Stability tests

Ultraviolet light (365 nm, 400 W) exposure was used to perform the accelerated light ageing tests. Low-temperature tests were performed by placing the sample in the freezer compartment of a commercial refrigerator for 24 h. High-temperature tests were performed by placing the sample on a hotplate with the temperature ranging from 50 to 250 °C for 24 h. Solvent resistance tests were performed by submerging the sample in a range of solvents for 24 h, including pure water, aqueous sodium hydroxide solution (1 mol l $^{-1}$ ), aqueous solution of acetic acid (1 mol l $^{-1}$ ), ethanol and hexadecane. Washing tests were performed by placing the sample into a commercial washing machine with the working time ranging from 10 to 150 min.

chunks.heading: Numerical simulation of meta-assemblies
chunks.text:
## Numerical simulation of meta-assemblies

The finite-difference time-domain simulation technique was performed to understand the near-field coupling between the incident light and meta-assemblies. The hemispherical meta-assembly was composed of nanospheres that were positioned in a close-packed arrangement. The meta-assembly was submerged in PDMS-like low-refractive-index media ( $n_{eff} = 1.41$ ). The upper layers of the meta-assembly were set as air-like environments ( $n_{eff} = 1$ ). A plane-wave source was placed 5 $\mu$ m above the top of the meta-assembly. The polarization direction of the incident wave was transverse-magnetic. To show the near-field mode profile, a two-dimensional field monitor (x-y plane monitor) was also inserted. The boundary condition for the z-direction was a standard perfect matched layer to eliminate unwanted reflection. Topological polarization was achieved by changing the meta-assembly morphology from a circular shape to quadrilaterals and octagons. C was set as the degree of circular polarization and E was set as the intensity of the electric field. $C \times E$ was set as the intensity of the circular polarization component. The polarization change was explored by changing the incident polarization angles. More simulation details are summarized in the Supplementary Materials.

chunks.heading: Characterizations
chunks.text:
## Characterizations

The dispersity of the colloidal nanoparticles was measured by a granulometer (ZetaPALS BI-90Plus, Brookhaven Instruments). Contact angles were measured using a contact angle measurement device (OCA20, DataPhysics) with the polymer droplet (2 $\mu$ l). The printed colloidal assemblies and microcavities were characterized by field-emission scanning electron microscopy (JEOL JSM-7500F) at an accelerating voltage of 5.0 kV. The optical micrographs were recorded by a bright-field microscope equipped with orthogonal polarizers (Nikon ECLIPSE Ti). The reflection spectra were measured by a micro-angle-resolved spectrum system (Ideaoptics) equipped with a high-sensitive spectrometer (NOVA, Ideaoptics). The reflection optical photographs and videos were captured using a Canon EOS 7D camera and a smartphone under vertical incident white light.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Biological systems achieve multifunctionality through the synergy of nanoscale building blocks and microscale morphological hierarchies, a multiscale structure that would be advantageous to implement in metamaterials $^{1-5}$ .

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: However, most artificial optical systems can only be fabricated on a single scale, facing the challenges of limited scalability, inadequate tunability and monotonous functionality $^{6-8}$ .

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Here we present a printable meta-assembly strategy that enables the fabrication of multiscale hierarchical optical architectures through continuous roll-to-roll (R2R) manufacturing.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: The meta-assembly comprises low-cost polystyrene (PS) nanoparticles periodically embedded in a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix, forming a nanolattice-based microconcave optical interface that enables precise integration of guided-wave and reflected-wave dispersion and interference $^{9-12}$ .

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: By optical coupling, distinct synergetic colouration is explored and experimentally realized with high designability and tunability.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Overcoming scalability constraints, metre-scale meta-assembly prints with single-pixel customization can be rapidly fabricated from the nanoscale building blocks, spanning seven orders of magnitude in length.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: The vibrant prints exhibit controlled colour separation and integration performances, along with environmental stability, showing potential for eco-friendly colouration, intelligent displays and information security.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: This work provides a versatile methodology for biologically inspired metamaterial construction by means of multiscale photonics research.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Colour, the most intuitive visual signature of the world, underpins fundamental interactions in biology $^{13,14}$ , technology $^{15,16}$ and culture $^{17,18}$ .

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Its origins lie in the light–matter interactions across multilength scales, which can be broadly categorized into chemical pigmentation colour (molecular absorption) and structural colour (optical interference/diffraction by microscale/nanoscale architectures) $^{2}$ .

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Although chemical dyes have dominated applications for millennia, the limitations of toxic chemical pollution $^{19-22}$ and colour fading $^{23,24}$ still persist as pressing challenges.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Thus, structural colour, as an eco-friendly colouration alternative, has emerged as a focal point in cutting-edge science and transformative technology, showcasing substantial potential to address both environmental and functional imperatives $^{25-29}$ .

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Nature stands as the quintessential architect of structural colouration, demonstrating elegant optical systems through hierarchical coupling of multiscale microstructures/nanostructures $^{2,5,30}$ and endowing organisms with resplendent chromatic displays and diverse crucial ecological functions $^{31-34}$ .

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Typical examples are Morpho butterflies $^{35}$ and Saharan ants $^{36}$ , which have evolved sophisticated hierarchical architectures that can synergize several optical effects (interference, scattering and so on) for brilliant colouration, alongside excellent heterosexual attraction and survival capabilities.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Despite decades of inspiration from the biological blueprints, translating these into artificial realizations remains highly challenging $^{37,38}$ , mainly because of the lack of validated multiscale optical models with scalable fabrication capability.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Present artificial colouration systems struggle to predict multiscale synergetic interactions or unify disparate chromogenic mechanisms $^{38-40}$ , thus failing to guide the rational design of hierarchical colouration structures.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Meanwhile, nanofabrication strategies for hierarchical architectures (for example, two-photon lithography) face critical trade-offs among cost, efficiency and scalability $^{37,41-44}$ .

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: Consequently, a unified multiscale optical platform with versatile fabrication is highly desirable.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: In this work, we present a printable meta-assembly strategy that enables the scalable fabrication of multiscale hierarchical optical architectures with distinct synergetic colouration performance.

spans.heading: Printable meta-assemblies enable synergetic colouration
spans.text: The meta-assembly model is designed with a microscale hemispherical

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: ## Article

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: configuration composed of hexagonal close-packed nanoparticles, forming a nanolattice-based microconcave interface.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: The nanolattice first defines a wavelength-selective photonic bandgap (PBG) $^{9}$ and the curved interface with refractive index contrast subsequently endows the meta-assembly with light localization capability by means of total internal reflections (TIRs) $^{10}$ (Supplementary Figs.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: 1–3; see Supplementary Discussions for details).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Through the ordered nano-arrangement on the curved interface, the meta-assembly achieves efficient multiscale optical interplay, enabling substantial field enhancement and dispersion in a single unit (Supplementary Fig. 4).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Then, to prepare the meta-assembly in batch, we develop a combined methodology called roll-to-roll additive nanoprinting (R2R-ANP) and a tailored manufacturing set-up, achieving the scalable and customized meta-assembly printing (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Figure 1a demonstrates the key R2R-ANP steps, including on-demand inkjet printing, blade coating and embedded transfer.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: First, digital images are designed into printing patterns, of which the spatial arrangement, size and density can be set as required with single-pixel resolution (Supplementary Fig. 5).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Then, using inkjet printing, the PS nanoparticle ink is precisely deposited on a hydrophobic and low-adhesion substrate to construct domed colloidal photonic crystals (DCPCs).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: The PS nanoparticles are selected as the building blocks owing to the matched refractive index, scalable synthesis capability and excellent stability that are essential for scalable R2R-ANP (Supplementary Figs.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: 6 and 7).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: After the ink dries, PS nanoparticles (for example, 216 nm in diameter) will self-assemble into the DCPC structures with green structural colour.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Subsequently, a layer of liquid PDMS is blade-coated on the DCPCs and cured by thermal polymerization.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Here the DCPCs are stably embedded in the PDMS matrix and interconnected using cross-linked networks.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Finally, on peeling and rolling the PDMS off the substrate, the interface profiles transform from domed to concave, thereby triggering the meta-assembly formation and size-dependent rim-centre co-colouration.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Consequently, the initially green prints exhibit rich colouration (Fig. 1a, bottom and Supplementary Fig. 8).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Spanning from nanoscale building blocks to microscale meta-assemblies, mesoscale arrays, and macroscale prints, the R2R-ANP approach bridges seven orders of magnitude in length, achieving the large-scale manufacturing of multiscale optical architectures (Fig. 1b).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Figure 1c shows the multiscale optical effects in the meta-assembly model.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: At the nanoscale, the periodic arrangement of PS nanoparticles ( $n_{\text{PS}} = 1.59$ ) within the PDMS matrix ( $n_{\text{PDMS}} = 1.41$ ) generates the PBG effect, inducing the wavelength-selective reflection and central colouration.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Meanwhile, the concave optical interface confines the incident light to propagate along the curved trajectories, guiding multibounce interference and colouration at the rim region.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Thus, the electric fields are spatially resolved and enhanced, manifesting distinct wavelength-dependent localization (Fig. 1d).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Furthermore, owing to phase retardation by TIR $^{45}$ , the capability of polarization conversion is introduced into the meta-assembly system (Supplementary Fig. 9), yielding annular imaging under crossed polarizers.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Notably, in contrast to photonic-crystal microspheres (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Figs.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: 10 and 11) and homogeneous polymer hemispheres (Supplementary Fig. 12), the meta-assembly exclusively exhibits a unique multiscale optical effect that is absent in these control samples.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Moreover, this optical performance demonstrates versatile tunability (Fig. 1f), with the TIR-based reflection shifting as the meta-assembly size increases.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: ## Principles for scalable R2R-ANP

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: As is well known, scalable fabrication imposes stringent demands on the throughput, yield and uniformity of the entire manufacturing process, with the following key issues being critical for scalable R2R-ANP (Fig. 2a).

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: First and foremost, continuous inkjet printing is essential.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Although inkjet printing provides on-demand patterning capabilities, it imposes stringent requirements on ink properties (for example, viscosities, surface tensions, boiling points) $^{46}$ .

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: To mitigate unstable jetting and nozzle clogging problems, we optimize the formamide-based colloidal ink (Supplementary Fig. 13), achieving stable, high-speed and high-resolution printing (Supplementary Figs.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Next, to freely construct the DCPC structure, ink droplets are designed to deposit on the hydrophobic and low-adhesion substrates (Fig. 2a, (1)), characterized by a large receding contact angle ( $\theta_{Rec} \approx 90^{\circ}$ ).

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: On such substrates, the ink droplets can continuously shrink at a constant $\theta_{Rec}$ , driving nanoparticles to self-assemble into DCPC structures, which are readily tuned by controlling nanoparticle concentration and printed ink-drop layers (Extended Data Fig. 2).

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Meanwhile, the optimal $\theta_{Rec}$ window for high-performance meta-assembly ranges from $80^{\circ}$ to $110^{\circ}$ , within which the meta-assemblies show pronounced rim enhancement (Fig. 2b).

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Furthermore, to expedite solvent evaporation, the substrate temperature is maintained at $50^{\circ}C$ throughout the processing.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: By using these optimized parameters, tens of millions of DCPCs with high resolution (403,225 dots per square inch) and exceptional uniformity are successfully fabricated (Supplementary Fig. 17), establishing a solid foundation for high-performance meta-assemblies.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: The following critical step involves the construction of stable microconcave optical interfaces.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: For pure nanoparticle assemblies, they exhibit inherent fragility owing to weak inter-particle interactions.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Thus, we design the composite optical interfaces by introducing PDMS matrix.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Experimentally, the PDMS prepolymer is directly coated onto the DCPC surface.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Thanks to its low surface energy, the prepolymer can freely diffuse into the voids between the nanoparticles and encapsulate the DCPCs while fully preserving the ordered nano-arrangements and domed morphology (Fig. 2a, (2)).

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: On prepolymer curing, the nanoparticles can be stably fixed by cross-linked networks, forming an integral composite that is embedded in the PDMS matrix (Fig. 2a, (3)).

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Thus, with the PDMS film peeled from the substrate and flipped, the meta-assemblies with robust optical interfaces directly form (Fig. 2a, (4)).

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Using this embedded transfer, all fabricated DCPCs can be converted into meta-assemblies with a $100\%$ yield, regardless of their number, size and distribution (Fig. 2c).

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Furthermore, the as-prepared meta-assemblies feature excellent size and colour uniformity (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 18), demonstrating great large-area potential.

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Experimentally, we fabricate a metre-scale film containing more than 40 million meta-assemblies, with the total number of nanoparticles exceeding $7 \times 10^{13}$ , which effectively validates the scalability of our strategy (Fig. 2e).

spans.heading: Principles for scalable R2R-ANP
spans.text: Furthermore, apart from circular meta-assemblies, diverse topological meta-assemblies can be readily fabricated by integrating R2R-ANP with heterogeneous wettability design (Supplementary Fig. 19 and Extended Data Fig. 3), greatly enriching the geometric diversity.

spans.text: ## Optical synergies in meta-assembly systems

spans.heading: Optical synergies in meta-assembly systems
spans.text: To exactly reveal the synergetic optical effects, a numerical analysis is performed on the basis of the built meta-assembly model.

spans.heading: Optical synergies in meta-assembly systems
spans.text: Given the mismatch between hexagonal lattice and curved hemisphere, we have first smoothed the interface perturbations, using an ordered nanolattice interface on the premise of computational accuracy.

spans.heading: Optical synergies in meta-assembly systems
spans.text: Unlike the predictable optical effects of single-scale structures, the meta-assembly enables non-trivial modulation of electromagnetic field distribution and light propagation.

spans.heading: Optical synergies in meta-assembly systems
spans.text: As illustrated in Fig. 3a–f, wavelength-dependent field enhancement and mode competition occur at the interface, owing to the interplay between different-scaled optical effects.

spans.heading: Optical synergies in meta-assembly systems
spans.text: Notably, at this wavelength, the field near the central boundary deflects leftward, whereas the rim field deflects rightward, exhibiting distinct interference cancellation in the overlap region.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Owing to the coexistence and interplay of multiscale optical effects, the meta-assembly system exhibits distinctive dispersion characteristics.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: As illustrated in the near-field to far-field dispersion profile (Fig. 3i,j), the central colouration is essentially invariant owing to strong wavelength selectivity and minimal angular dispersion, whereas the rim region exhibits a pronounced angular-dependent colour variation.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Rim dispersion originates from the pronounced optical path difference during TIR-confined propagation when light impinges on the rim regions, thereby inducing the mutual interference of electromagnetic waves.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Because short wavelengths first meet the interference condition, their intensities are preferentially enhanced (for example, blue and purple).

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: As the optical path difference increases, the interference of long wavelengths is enhanced, with yellow, orange and similar hues gradually emerging.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Notably, owing to the filtering effect by PBGs, the corresponding intensity is largely suppressed.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: In the near field, this wavelength dependence is indistinguishable.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: As the wave propagates into the far-field region, the interfacial confinement gradually attenuates, whereas the spatial phase coherence of the scattered light is markedly enhanced.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Consequently, the optical field distribution becomes stably established, with the specific wavelength components exhibiting a more uniform propagation direction.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Correspondingly, the meta-assembly shows a constant PBG-dominated reflection in the central region and intense wavelength-dependent scattering near the interface, causing the spatially varied colour distribution.

spans.text: Notably, with the change of receiving angle, the structural colour evolves from stable green to intense iridescence as the dominant optical mechanism transitions from pure PBG to coupled PBG–TIR and ultimately to exclusive TIR.

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: This dynamic transformation is further corroborated by angle-resolved reflection spectra: at near-normal reflection angles, narrow PBG spectral peaks are initially detected; as the angle increases incrementally, the PBG peak gradually attenuates, whereas the TIR peak becomes increasingly prominent, showing marked variations across a broad visible spectral range (Fig. 3n).

spans.heading: Article

spans.heading: Article
spans.text: Furthermore, tailored adjustments to either the lattice constant or meta-assembly size can change the rim colour spatial distribution, thereby highlighting the versatile multiscale tunability (Supplementary Fig. 20).

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: ## Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Notably, the pronounced multiscale optical interplay within the meta-assembly system offers a facile approach to tailoring its structural colouration.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Accordingly, we collect the spectral data at specific spatial regions of the meta-assembly and convert the spectra into intuitive chromatic colours, first illustrating the distinct colour synergy from parts to the whole.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Subsequently, the colour tunability corresponding to structural changes is systematically demonstrated.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: As shown in Fig. 4a, reducing the meta-assembly diameter ( $D_{m}$ ) from $80 \times D_{n}$ to $40 \times D_{n}$ (in which $D_{n}$ is the photonic lattice constant, 220 nm) triggers a distinct rim colour transition from orange to blue owing to the changed TIR paths, whereas the central colour remains green.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Accordingly, the overall colour shifts slightly from yellowish green to cyan.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Conversely, increasing $D_{n}$ from 220 nm to 240 nm ( $D_{m} = 40 \times D_{n}$ ) triggers a prominent redshift in the central colour and a slight modulation on the rim colour owing to the changed photonic lattice.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: At this time, the overall colour is vividly shifted from cyan–green to pink.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Such multiscale colour modulation can be further validated in the meta-assemblies with different multiscale structural parameters (Fig. 4b).

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Moreover, to fully illustrate the quantitative correspondence between colour and multiscale structures, we construct the centre, rim and overall colouration libraries with varied $D_{m}$ and $D_{n}$ (Fig. 4c) and experimentally map the meta-assemblies from the microscale (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 4) and macroscale (Supplementary Fig. 21), directly illustrating the structure–colour correlation.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: As shown, the centre colour exhibits a clear linear dependence on $D_{n}$ , with a distinct redshift observed as the $D_{n}$ increases.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Furthermore, the rim colour gradually shifts from short-wavelength hues (for example, blue and purple) to long-wavelength hues (for example, orange and red) as the $D_{m}$ increases.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Because the colour variations at the rim and centre both contribute to the overall colouration, the meta-assembly naturally features the multiscale tunability, thus enabling broadband and refined colour modulation.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Besides tailoring structural parameters, the meta-assembly-based macroscopic colouration also exhibits printing-enabled tunability (Fig. 4e–h and Extended Data Fig. 5).

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: First, the reflection intensity is facile to adjust with the regulation of meta-assembly density (Supplementary Fig. 22).

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Second, meta-assemblies with different $D_{n}$ and $D_{m}$ can be integrated and printed to achieve the predefined macroscopic colour mixing.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: As shown in Fig. 4e–g, through multinozzle inkjet printing of different nanoparticle inks, the meta-assemblies with characteristic red, green and blue central colours are patterned in an orderly manner, yielding the macroscopic white colouration.

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Furthermore, through designed layer-by-layer processing, the meta-assemblies with different sizes can be readily integrated using a single nanoparticle ink, enabling the facile fabrication of colourful panel and print (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 5g).

spans.heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.semantic_heading: Rich colour tunability of the meta-assembly
spans.text: Overall, the combined structural and printing tunability endows the meta-assembly system with full-scale colour designability, thus showcasing substantial potential for custom-tailored structural-colour applications.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: ## Macroscopic synergetic colouration

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: Not only in individual meta-assemblies, the synergetic colouration can also be readily scaled up to the macroscale by controlling the illumination conditions.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: As illustrated in Fig. 5a,b, with an oblique light incidence into the meta-assembly, the PBG-dominated Bragg reflection and TIR-dominated retroreflection will be spatially separated, thereby inducing the colour separation at the macroscale.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: This illumination-controlled reflection and retroreflection afford the macroscopic meta-assembly colouration with enhanced tunability, for which the colour output can be precisely modulated by tailoring the Bragg angle ( $\theta$ , reflection mode) and the light-viewing distance (D, retroreflection mode).

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: Notably, when the single oblique incident beam is switched to dual-beam cooperative illumination, the reflection and retroreflection can be effectively integrated to achieve the mode combination and colour mixing.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: As shown in Fig. 5c, the reflective green and retroreflective blue are uniformly mixed, inducing the cyan generation.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: Using different-sized meta-assemblies, a rich palette of mixed structural colours is achieved (Supplementary Fig. 23).

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: Especially, when the print composed of patterned meta-assemblies is applied, it can yield a more intriguing synergetic colouration (Fig. 5d).

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: The print is specifically designed with dual-sized meta-assemblies (13 and 30 $\mu$ m in diameter) that are composed of the 216-nm-diameter nanoparticles.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: In reflection mode, the print only exhibits an overall uniform green image.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: By contrast, the retroreflection mode yields a colourful appearance arising from the TIR-based size-dependent colouration.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: Finally, under dual-beam cooperative illumination, the reflection and retroreflection are simultaneously excited and superimposed, inducing gradational chromatic colours and a soft visual appearance.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: The unique synergetic colouration endows the meta-assemblies with substantial potential in security identification.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: To further validate its real-world applicability, we systematically characterize the stability of meta-assemblies against light irradiation, thermal stress, solvent exposure, washing and mechanical deformation.

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: Benefiting from the robust bonding between nanoparticles and the PDMS matrix, the meta-assemblies exhibit remarkable overall environmental and mechanical stabilities (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 24).

spans.heading: Macroscopic synergetic colouration
spans.text: Notably, the meta-assembly prints can be conformally attached to various substrates, including paper, microchips and curved glass surfaces, which are highly advantageous for the reliable and durable security functionality (Supplementary Fig. 25).

spans.heading: Conclusions
spans.text: ## Conclusions

spans.heading: Conclusions
spans.text: In summary, we have presented a unified metamaterial platform featuring scalable fabrication capability and multiscale structural designability, enabling the customized and low-cost manufacturing of hierarchical optical architectures.

spans.heading: Conclusions
spans.text: The developed meta-assembly model endows the common polymer building blocks with multiscale optical activity, achieving effective optical coupling and synergetic colouration within a single unit.

spans.heading: Conclusions
spans.text: Its facile configuration, coupled with a tailored R2R-ANP protocol, yields the continuous R2R production of macroscopic meta-assembly prints with single-pixel resolution, thus offering a feasible route for the lab-to-fab translation of optical metamaterials.

spans.heading: Conclusions
spans.text: Moreover, the meta-assembly prints enable a more straightforward realization of synergistic optical performance while featuring excellent stability, thus offering substantial application potential for practical colouration scenarios ranging from information security to intelligent displays.

spans.heading: Conclusions
spans.text: Collectively, this printable meta-assembly strategy resolves the trade-off between optical functionality and engineering performance, providing key insights for multiscale photonics research.

spans.heading: Conclusions
spans.text: Furthermore, integrating intrinsic material properties into the meta-assembly model holds great promise for unlocking more intriguing functionalities.
